verdict.summary:
HOURS-OF-SERVICE LIMITS FOR A PROPERTY-CARRYING CMV DRIVER — 49 CFR 395.3(a)

SCOPE. Property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, operated in the United States, subject to the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations, no exemption or exception (395.1) invoked, current text of the rule. Under these conditions the three answers are 10, 14, and 11 hours. Passenger-carrying vehicles are governed by 395.5 and use different numbers (see Section 5); the property-carrying scoping is load-bearing.

1. ANSWERS

Ask 1 — Minimum consecutive off-duty time before driving: 10 consecutive hours off duty.
Ask 2 — Hours after coming on duty at which driving must stop: 14 consecutive hours.
Ask 3 — Total driving permitted inside that period: 11 hours.

2. OPERATIVE TEXT (49 CFR 395.3(a), current)

"(a) Except as otherwise provided in 395.1, no motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, unless the driver complies with the following requirements:
  (1) Start of work shift. A driver may not drive without first taking 10 consecutive hours off duty;
  (2) 14-hour period. A driver may not drive after a period of 14 consecutive hours after coming on-duty following 10 consecutive hours off-duty.
  (3) Driving time and interruptions of driving periods—
    (i) Driving time. A driver may drive a total of 11 hours during the period specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section.
    (ii) Interruption of driving time. Except for drivers who qualify for either of the short-haul exceptions in 395.1(e)(1) or (2), driving is not permitted if more than 8 hours of driving time have passed without at least a consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status. A consecutive 30-minute interruption of driving status may be satisfied either by off-duty, sleeper berth or on-duty not driving time or by a combination of off-duty, sleeper berth and on-duty not driving time."

Source basis: eCFR current text of 395.3 and the 2024 and 2025 govinfo PDFs of 49 CFR part 395, which agree verbatim; amendment history 76 FR 81188 (Dec. 27, 2011), as amended 78 FR 58485, 78 FR 64181, 84 FR 48081, 85 FR 33452 (June 1, 2020). The 2004 version (68 FR 22516) used different wording — "more than 11 cumulative hours following 10 consecutive hours off duty" and "after the end of the 14th hour after coming on duty" — but the same three numbers, so the answers are stable across versions even though the phrasing changed.

3. MEASUREMENT CONVENTIONS — READ THESE WITH THE NUMBERS

(a) Ask 1: the 10 hours must be consecutive and must be off duty (off-duty or sleeper-berth status, not on-duty-not-driving). It is a precondition to driving, not a daily average; it may not be assembled from scattered shorter breaks. The one codified way to satisfy the 10-hour requirement in pieces is the sleeper-berth split in 395.1(g), which is outside the plain 395.3(a) answer.

(b) Ask 2: the 14 hours run from the moment the driver comes on duty after the 10-hour break. It is elapsed wall-clock time, not accumulated on-duty time. Off-duty, sleeper-berth, meal, fueling, or waiting time occurring inside the window does NOT pause it and does NOT extend it. A driver who comes on duty at 06:00 may not drive at any time after 20:00 that same day, regardless of how much of the intervening 14 hours was spent not driving. The regulation prohibits driving after the window closes; it does not force the driver off duty, and on-duty-not-driving work after hour 14 is not itself a 395.3(a) violation.

(c) Ask 3: the 11 hours is a cap on driving time inside the 14-hour period. It is not additive to the window and it cannot be banked or shifted into a later window. Because 11 < 14, every compliant day contains at least 3 hours of the window that are not driving; a driver who has driven 11 hours must stop driving even if only, say, 12 hours of the window have elapsed.

(d) Interaction of the three: the binding constraint is whichever comes first — 11 hours of driving accumulated, or 14 hours of elapsed window. Both terminate driving. The 30-minute interruption rule in (a)(3)(ii) is a third, separate constraint: driving is not permitted once more than 8 hours of driving time have elapsed without a consecutive interruption of at least 30 minutes (satisfiable by off-duty, sleeper berth, on-duty-not-driving, or any combination). Because 8 < 11, a full 11-hour driving day necessarily contains at least one qualifying interruption.

4. WORKED EXAMPLE (internally consistent with all three values)

Window opens: driver comes on duty 06:00 after 10 consecutive hours off duty. Window closes at 20:00.
- 06:00–06:30 on duty not driving (pre-trip) — driving time 0.0, window elapsed 0.5
- 06:30–10:30 driving — driving time 4.0
- 10:30–11:00 off duty, 30 min — satisfies the (a)(3)(ii) interruption before the 8-hour driving mark is passed
- 11:00–15:00 driving — driving time 8.0
- 15:00–15:30 on duty not driving (loading) — second 30-minute interruption; driving time still 8.0
- 15:30–18:30 driving — driving time 11.0  ← 11-hour cap reached
- 18:30–20:00 on duty not driving — permitted, but no driving
- At 20:00 the 14-hour window closes.
Result: 11 hours driving, 14-hour window used, no violation. Note that the driver could not have driven to 20:30 to use the remaining window: the 11-hour cap bound first at 18:30. Conversely, a driver who took a 2-hour off-duty lunch inside the day would still face the 20:00 wall, because the break does not extend the window.

5. ADJACENT RULES THAT INTERACT (not answers to the three asks)

- 395.3(b): no driving after 60 hours on duty in 7 consecutive days (carrier not operating every day) or 70 hours on duty in 8 consecutive days (carrier operating every day). This is a cumulative multi-day cap, independent of the 11/14 figures, and can bind before either of them.
- 395.3(c): a 7- or 8-day period may be ended by the beginning of an off-duty period of 34 or more consecutive hours (the "restart").
- 395.1(g): sleeper-berth pairing (7+ hours in the sleeper plus a 2+ hour off-duty/sleeper period, totaling 10) can exclude the longer period from the 14-hour calculation — the principal lawful way the 14-hour wall moves.
- 395.1(b): adverse driving conditions may extend the 11-hour driving limit and the 14-hour window by up to 2 hours; the driver may not drive after the 16th hour.
- 395.1(e): short-haul/air-mile exceptions, which among other things relieve the 30-minute interruption requirement and use a 14-hour duty window with a 16-hour extension in some cases.
- 395.1(h): Alaska — property-carrying drivers there are subject to 15 hours driving following 10 consecutive hours off duty, a 20-hour outer on-duty limit, and 70/80-hour weekly caps instead of the figures above.
- 395.5: passenger-carrying vehicles — 10 hours driving following 8 consecutive hours off duty, and no driving after 15 hours on duty. Different numbers; the answers in Section 1 do not apply to them.
- 395.8 / subpart B: the record-of-duty-status and ELD obligations that make the above auditable.

6. HOW THE NUMBERS WERE VERIFIED AGAINST EACH OTHER

- Driving cap (11) does not exceed the window (14): consistent, and the 3-hour residual is stated explicitly.
- Interruption trigger (8 hours of driving) is below the driving cap (11): consistent, and the worked example includes two interruptions, so no example in this deliverable violates a limit the deliverable itself sets.
- Off-duty requirement (10 consecutive hours) precedes and starts the 14-hour window: the ordering in the worked example (off duty until 06:00, window opens at 06:00) matches the regulation's "after coming on-duty following 10 consecutive hours off-duty."
- No figure here is drawn from guidance or enforcement policy; all three come from the regulatory text quoted in Section 2, which is identical in the eCFR and the 2024 and 2025 printed CFR volumes.

verdict.summary:
# Rescission deadlines under 12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(i)

## Short answer

1. **Baseline deadline (ask 1).** The consumer may exercise the right to rescind **until midnight of the third business day following the last of three events**: (a) consummation, (b) delivery of the § 1026.23(b) notice of the right to rescind, or (c) delivery of all material disclosures. It is *whichever occurs last* — so a late notice or late material disclosures restarts and extends the window; an early notice or early disclosures does not shorten it below three business days after consummation.

2. **Never-delivered notice or material disclosures (ask 2).** If the required notice or the material disclosures are **not delivered**, the right expires **3 years after consummation** — but that is a ceiling, not a fixed term: it expires at the **earliest** of (a) 3 years after consummation, (b) transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or (c) sale of the property.

Both answers are read directly off the operative sentence, quoted verbatim below.

## Governing text (verbatim)

**12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(i):**

> "The consumer may exercise the right to rescind until midnight of the third business day following consummation, delivery of the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever occurs last. If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first. In the case of certain administrative proceedings, the rescission period shall be extended in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act."

**12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(ii)** (defines the second trigger's content):

> "For purposes of this paragraph (a)(3), the term 'material disclosures' means the required disclosures of the annual percentage rate, the finance charge, the amount financed, the total of payments, the payment schedule, and the disclosures and limitations referred to in §§ 1026.32(c) and (d) and 1026.43(g)."

**12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(2)** (what counts as exercising the right — this is what "until midnight" is measured against):

> "To exercise the right to rescind, the consumer shall notify the creditor of the rescission by mail, telegram or other means of written communication. Notice is considered given when mailed, when filed for telegraphic transmission or, if sent by other means, when delivered to the creditor's designated place of business."

Supplement I, comment 23(a)(3)-1.i restates the rule as running "for 3 business days from the last of 3 events": consummation; delivery of all material disclosures; delivery of the required rescission notice.

## Ask 1 — mechanics of the three-business-day period

**Trigger set.** Three candidate events. The period does not start until the *last* of them has occurred. Practically:

| Situation | Period runs from |
|---|---|
| Notice and material disclosures delivered at or before consummation | Consummation |
| Notice and disclosures delivered *after* consummation (permitted — see comment 23(b) ¶4: the notice "need not be given before consummation ... the rescission period will not begin to run until the notice is given") | The later delivery date |
| Notice timely, material disclosures late (or vice versa) | The later of the two deliveries |

**Endpoint.** Midnight of the third business day counted from the last trigger. "Midnight" means the end of that calendar day, not the start.

**Manner of exercise.** Under § 1026.23(a)(2) the consumer need not have the notice *in the creditor's hands* by the deadline: mailing it, filing it for telegraphic transmission, or delivering it to the creditor's designated place of business within the period is enough. Comment 23(a)(3)-1.ii.B says exactly this: "The consumer must place the rescission notice in the mail, file it for telegraphic transmission, or deliver it to the creditor's place of business within that period in order to exercise the right." Any one of multiple consumers with the right may exercise it, and that exercise is effective for all — § 1026.23(a)(4).

**Worked examples (from comment 23(a)(3)-1.ii, verified against the rule):**

- Consummation Friday, June 1; disclosures and rescission notice delivered Thursday, May 31. Last event = June 1. Third business day after June 1 (Saturday and Sunday excluded) = Tuesday, June 5. Period expires **midnight Tuesday, June 5**. ✓
- Disclosures delivered and transaction consummated Friday, June 1; rescission notice delivered Monday, June 4. Last event = June 4. Third business day after June 4 = Thursday, June 7. Period expires **midnight Thursday, June 7**. ✓

**Definitional note (flagged — not in the sourced excerpts).** For rescission purposes, "business day" is defined in § 1026.2(a)(6) as **all calendar days except Sundays and the legal public holidays listed in 5 U.S.C. § 6103(a)** (New Year's Day, MLK Day, Washington's Birthday, Memorial Day, Independence Day, Labor Day, Columbus Day, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas) — i.e., *Saturdays count* for rescission, unlike the general "open for substantially all business functions" definition used elsewhere in Regulation Z. This definition was not present in the fetched passages and should be confirmed against § 1026.2(a)(6) before use in a live deadline computation. It does not affect either reported value.

## Ask 2 — the never-delivered case

**Rule.** If the required notice or the material disclosures are never delivered, the short three-business-day window never starts, and the right instead survives to the **earliest** of:

1. **3 years after consummation** (the ceiling reported as the answer);
2. **transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property**; or
3. **sale of the property**.

**How to read it.** The 3-year figure is the outer limit only when none of the other two events has occurred. A sale or a transfer of all the consumer's interest cuts the right off earlier, even inside the three years. Conversely, the three-year date is not shortened by the consumer's continued occupancy or by the creditor's forbearance. This is also the structure of the statute: TILA § 125(f), 15 U.S.C. § 1635(f), provides that the right "shall expire three years after the date of consummation of the transaction or upon the sale of the property, whichever occurs first" where the required information or notice was not delivered.

**Why "not delivered" is the trigger, not "defectively delivered."** The clause is keyed to non-delivery. A delivered-but-inaccurate disclosure is analyzed under the accuracy/tolerance provisions (§ 1026.23(g)–(h)) and the material-disclosure definition in (a)(3)(ii), not under the 3-year clause. Note also that a disclosure is "material" for this purpose only if it is one of the enumerated items in (a)(3)(ii): APR, finance charge, amount financed, total of payments, payment schedule, and the § 1026.32(c) and (d) and § 1026.43(g) disclosures and limitations. Omission of something outside that list does not trigger the 3-year tail.

**Administrative-proceeding extension.** The final sentence of (a)(3)(i) extends the rescission period in certain administrative proceedings under TILA § 125(f). This is a narrow carve-out and is outside the two values reported; it should be checked separately if the transaction is in an administrative enforcement posture.

## Scope boundaries that qualify both answers

- **Only covered transactions.** The right exists only where a security interest is or will be retained or acquired in the consumer's **principal dwelling** and the consumer's ownership interest is subject to it — § 1026.23(a)(1).
- **Exempt transactions, § 1026.23(f):** residential mortgage transactions; refinancings/consolidations by the same creditor of credit already secured by the principal dwelling (except as to new money); transactions where a state agency is the creditor; subsequent advances in a series where notice and material disclosures were given; renewals of optional insurance premiums. No rescission right, so no deadline, for these.
- **Added security interest, § 1026.23(a)(1):** adding a security interest to an existing obligation is itself a rescindable transaction as to the added interest only; the creditor need not deliver new material disclosures, and **delivery of the required notice alone begins the rescission period**.
- **Waiver, § 1026.23(e):** where the consumer waives the three-day waiting period after receiving proper notice, the baseline period is displaced by the waiver.
- **Disclosure of the expiry date is itself required, § 1026.23(b)(1)(v):** the creditor must state "the date the rescission period expires" in the notice. That date must be computed on the assumptions above (last of the three events, third business day, midnight).

## Verification status and caveats

- The quoted rule text is identical across the eCFR subpart C page, the eCFR subpart B mirror, the GovInfo 2025 CFR XML, and the CFPB's own reproduction; comment 23(a)(3)-1 and comment 23(b) ¶4 come from the CFPB reproduction of Supplement I.
- The § 1026.2(a)(6) business-day definition is **flagged as unsourced** from the fetched excerpts (see above) and should be confirmed before being used to compute a specific calendar date.
- Case-law glosses (e.g., *Jesinoski v. Countrywide Home Loans*, 574 U.S. 259 (2015), holding that written notice within the period effects rescission without a suit) are **outside the regulation text** and outside the scope assumed for this answer; they are noted only so a reader does not mistake the regulatory period for the whole of the doctrine.
- No factual record for any particular transaction was supplied, so this states the rule's deadlines, not a computed date for a specific loan. To compute an actual date: identify the last of the three trigger events, count three business days forward excluding Sundays and federal holidays, and the period ends at midnight of that day; if any required notice or material disclosure was never delivered, compute the earlier of the three-year anniversary of consummation and any sale or transfer of all the consumer's interest.

verdict.summary:
ANNUAL OCCUPATIONAL DOSE LIMITS FOR ADULT WORKERS — 10 CFR § 20.1201(a)

Source of record: 10 CFR § 20.1201, 'Occupational dose limits for adults,' as published in the current eCFR (Title 10, Chapter I, Part 20, Subpart C) and as printed in the 2024 and 2025 annual editions of 10 CFR Part 20 (govinfo). The three editions agree verbatim; the figures below are the regulation's own, including its parenthetical SI conversions.

1. ANSWER TABLE

| Quantity (regulatory term) | Annual limit (rem) | Annual limit (Sv) | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total effective dose equivalent (TEDE), whole body | 5 rems | 0.05 Sv | § 20.1201(a)(1)(i) |
| Lens of the eye — lens dose equivalent | 15 rems | 0.15 Sv | § 20.1201(a)(2)(i) |
| Skin of the whole body — shallow-dose equivalent | 50 rem | 0.5 Sv | § 20.1201(a)(2)(ii) |

Unit convention: 1 Sv = 100 rem. Conversions check exactly against the regulation's printed parentheticals: 5 rem ÷ 100 = 0.05 Sv; 15 rem ÷ 100 = 0.15 Sv; 50 rem ÷ 100 = 0.5 Sv. No rounding is introduced by this document; the values are as the rule states them.

2. GOVERNING TEXT (verbatim, current eCFR)

§ 20.1201 Occupational dose limits for adults.

"(a) The licensee shall control the occupational dose to individual adults, except for planned special exposures under § 20.1206, to the following dose limits.

(1) An annual limit, which is the more limiting of—

(i) The total effective dose equivalent being equal to 5 rems (0.05 Sv); or

(ii) The sum of the deep-dose equivalent and the committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue other than the lens of the eye being equal to 50 rems (0.5 Sv).

(2) The annual limits to the lens of the eye, to the skin of the whole body, and to the skin of the extremities, which are:

(i) A lens dose equivalent of 15 rems (0.15 Sv), and

(ii) A shallow-dose equivalent of 50 rem (0.5 Sv) to the skin of the whole body or to the skin of any extremity."

Source history line as published: [56 FR 23396, May 21, 1991, as amended at 60 FR 20185, Apr. 25, 1995; 63 FR 39482, July 23, 1998; 67 FR 16304, Apr. 5, 2002; 72 FR 68059, Dec. 4, 2007]. The lens figure of 15 rems (0.15 Sv) is the value in force following the 2007 amendment and is unchanged in the current eCFR and the 2024/2025 CFR printings.

3. INTERPRETIVE POINTS A COMPLIANCE ENGINEER MUST NOT COLLAPSE

(a) The whole-body limit is not a flat 5 rem in all cases. § 20.1201(a)(1) is a 'more limiting of' test between (i) TEDE = 5 rems and (ii) deep-dose equivalent plus committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue other than the lens = 50 rems. The 5 rem TEDE figure is the answer to the whole-body question, but it is applied as one of two parallel criteria, whichever binds first.

(b) The skin figure and the organ figure are both 50 rems but are different quantities and must not be conflated. The skin limit is a shallow-dose equivalent (§ 20.1201(a)(2)(ii)); per § 20.1201(c) it is 'the dose averaged over the contiguous 10 square centimeters of skin receiving the highest exposure.' The 50 rem in § 20.1201(a)(1)(ii) is a deep-dose equivalent plus committed dose equivalent to an organ or tissue. Numerically equal, dimensionally distinct.

(c) The lens limit is a lens dose equivalent, a separate deterministic limit — not part of the TEDE summation and not the 'organ other than the lens of the eye' term in (a)(1)(ii), which expressly excludes the lens.

(d) Scope boundaries. The limits above are for adult workers (an adult is an individual 18 or more years of age, § 20.1003) in general occupational exposure. Excluded by the rule's own terms: planned special exposures under § 20.1206; minors, whose limits are 10 percent of the adult values (§ 20.1207); and the embryo/fetus limit (§ 20.1208). The skin of the extremities shares the same 50 rem shallow-dose equivalent as the skin of the whole body and is not separately reported here.

(e) Currency note, stated as context only and not as an alternate answer: the lens-of-eye limit has been the subject of international (ICRP) and domestic discussion, and the 15 rem (0.15 Sv) value is what the current, in-force text states. Any future amendment would change this answer; the citation history line above is the mechanism for detecting that.

4. HOW TO APPLY (compliance use)

For each monitored adult, demonstrate compliance against all three simultaneously: (i) TEDE for the year ≤ 5 rem (0.05 Sv) or the organ criterion of (a)(1)(ii) ≤ 50 rem (0.5 Sv), whichever is more limiting; (ii) lens dose equivalent for the year ≤ 15 rem (0.15 Sv); (iii) shallow-dose equivalent to the skin of the whole body for the year ≤ 50 rem (0.5 Sv). Where external exposure is measured with a personal monitoring device, the deep-dose equivalent is used in place of the effective dose equivalent unless an NRC-approved dosimetry method determines EDE, and the assigned deep-dose equivalent must be for the part of the body receiving the highest exposure (§ 20.1201(c)). The limit is reduced by occupational dose received in the year while employed by any other person (§ 20.1201(f), § 20.2104(e)).

5. VERIFICATION PERFORMED

- Every numeric limit above was read directly from the regulation's text in four independent renderings (current eCFR section page, current eCFR Subpart C, CFR 2024 XML, CFR 2025 XML, and the CFR 2025 Part 20 PDF); all agree.
- Each rem figure was checked against its printed SI parenthetical using 1 Sv = 100 rem; all three agree exactly with no rounding.
- No value stated in this document exceeds, or is inconsistent with, any threshold stated in this document.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER TO BOTH ASKS (29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1), Unprotected Sides and Edges)

Controlling text (quoted verbatim from the current eCFR section page and the GovInfo PDF of 29 CFR 1926.501; identical in all fetched sources):

  '(b)(1) Unprotected sides and edges. Each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal and vertical surface) with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems.'

ASK 1 — HEIGHT: 6 feet (1.8 m) above a lower level.
- The trigger is '6 feet (1.8 m) or more.' Exactly 6 ft (1.8 m) is at or above the threshold and therefore requires protection; there is no tolerance band and no rounding allowance in the text.
- The dimension is measured from the walking/working surface on which the employee stands down to the lower level — not from the employee's body, not from the top of a guardrail, and not from the toe of a slope.
- The regulated surface is defined parenthetically as a 'walking/working surface (horizontal and vertical surface),' so the duty applies to vertical surfaces as well as floors, decks, roofs and platforms.
- 'Unprotected side or edge' means a side or edge without a compliant guardrail system or equivalent barrier; if the edge is already guarded by a system meeting 1926.502(b), no further protection is owed.

ASK 2 — SYSTEMS: guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems.
- These three are alternatives, joined by 'or.' Providing any one of them, erected/used in accordance with 1926.502, satisfies the paragraph. There is no requirement to provide more than one.
- Each must meet the criteria of 1926.502: guardrails in 1926.502(b) (toprail 42 in. ±3 in., midrail, 200 lb load, etc.), safety nets in 1926.502(c) (installation, drop distance, mesh, certification), personal fall arrest systems in 1926.502(d) (full-body harness, anchor strength, free-fall and deceleration limits, prompt rescue). Section 1926.501(a)(1) makes this mandatory: 'All fall protection required by this section shall conform to the criteria set forth in 1926.502 of this subpart.'

WHAT DOES NOT SATISFY 1926.501(b)(1) — scope boundaries a safety engineer must police:
- The paragraph contains NO infeasibility/greater-hazard exception and does NOT authorize a fall protection plan under 1926.502(k). The exception and the 502(k) fall protection plan appear in (b)(2)(i) for leading edges; the accompanying 'presumption of feasibility' note is attached to (b)(2), not (b)(1). Do not carry that exception over to unprotected sides and edges.
- Controlled access zones, warning lines, safety monitoring systems, covers, and positioning device systems are NOT listed options under (b)(1). They are authorized only where another paragraph of (b) names them — e.g., (b)(4) holes (covers), (b)(5) formwork/reinforcing steel (positioning device systems), (b)(9) overhand bricklaying (controlled access zone), (b)(10) low-slope roofing (warning line/safety monitoring in combination). None of those substitutions may be used to discharge the (b)(1) duty.
- (b)(15) is the residual catch-all for walking/working surfaces not addressed in (b)(1)-(b)(14) and lists the same three systems; it does not widen the (b)(1) menu.

EFFECTIVE-DATE / VERSION CHECK: The current eCFR text (fetched 2026-11-15) and the GovInfo 'most recent' PDF both still state 6 feet (1.8 m) and the same three systems for (b)(1). Nothing in the retrieved current text changes this threshold or this list. The 2012 printed edition reads identically. Conclusion: the answer is stable across the historical and current text; no phased compliance date alters it.

SELECTION AND IMPLEMENTATION GUIDANCE (safety-engineering judgment, subordinate to the rule):
1. Prefer the passive control. Where the edge is fixed and predictable, a guardrail system is the first choice: it protects every exposed person continuously, needs no donning, and imposes no rescue dependency. Safety nets are second (collective, but require certified installation, drop-height and clearance checks, and removal-from-net procedures). Personal fall arrest systems are the last of the three for routine edge exposure because they are active, require trained users, and require prompt rescue.
2. If PFAS is selected: full-body harness with attachment at the back D-ring; anchorage at 5,000 lb per employee attached or designed by a qualified person per 1926.502(d)(15); lanyard/energy absorber configured to keep free fall within 1926.502(d)(16) limits; no body belts; prompt rescue of a fallen employee provided for per 1926.502(d)(20); anchor points and system inspected before each use.
3. Training: each employee exposed to the hazard must be trained per 1926.503 on the systems in use, the hazards, and the procedures, and retrained when systems or workplace conditions change.
4. Verify surface adequacy: 1926.501(a)(2) requires the employer to determine that walking/working surfaces have the strength and structural integrity to support employees safely before work is permitted.

VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (how the answer is applied and audited on a real site):
Step 1 — For each exposed side/edge, measure the vertical distance from the working surface to the nearest lower level; record the measurement and the measurement point on the survey/plan.
Step 2 — If the measured distance is 6 ft (1.8 m) or more, mark the edge as requiring protection under 1926.501(b)(1); if less, document the measured value so the determination is defensible, and still evaluate other hazards (falling objects under (c), ladders, scaffolds under Subpart L).
Step 3 — Record which of the three systems is provided, the 1926.502 criteria it is built to, the installer/competent person, the inspection date, and the training record for affected employees.
Step 4 — Re-verify whenever the edge geometry, working surface, or lower level changes (e.g., excavation backfill raising the lower level, decking added) — the trigger is dynamic, not a one-time determination.

ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER:
- Assumed: private-sector construction work in OSHA federal jurisdiction, so 29 CFR Part 1926 Subpart M governs. State-plan states may impose stricter requirements (and a few do for specific construction operations); the applicable state plan must be checked before relying on 6 ft as the site criterion. No state numeric threshold is asserted here.
- Assumed: the general case under (b)(1), not the special cases in (b)(2) through (b)(15) (leading edges, holes, formwork, ramps, excavations, dangerous equipment, bricklaying, roofing, wall openings), which carry their own system lists and, in some cases, their own exceptions.
- If a specific operation falls under one of those other paragraphs, that paragraph controls for that exposure; (b)(1) remains the rule for plain unprotected sides and edges.

verdict.summary:
REGULATION 4(1), WORKING TIME REGULATIONS 1998 (SI 1998/1833) — LIMIT AND ROUTE OUT

SCOPE NOTE (function: Legal). This is a statement of the general legal position under the regulation as it currently stands (England & Wales, Scotland; reg 4 is marked E+W+S). It is not advice on a particular worker, contract or workplace, and it does not cover the separate regimes for young workers, night workers, excluded sectors, mobile workers, doctors in training or offshore work beyond the flags given in section 4.

=====================================================================
1. THE LIMIT — 48 HOURS PER SEVEN DAYS, AVERAGED
=====================================================================

Current text of reg 4(1) (latest revised version, as amended):

  "4.—(1) [Unless his employer has first obtained the worker's agreement in writing to perform such work], a worker's working time, including overtime, in any reference period which is applicable in his case shall not exceed an average of 48 hours for each seven days."

The figure is therefore 48 hours for each seven days. Three features of that figure matter:

(a) It is an AVERAGE, not a weekly cap. Reg 4(1) speaks of the average "in any reference period which is applicable in his case". A worker may lawfully work more than 48 hours in a given week, or in several weeks, provided the average across the reference period does not exceed 48 hours per seven days.

(b) OVERTIME COUNTS. The words "including overtime" are express and were in the regulation as made. All working time counts, whether the overtime is contractual, guaranteed, voluntary, paid or unpaid.

(c) "WORKING TIME" is the defined term (reg 2), not simply hours at the premises; it is time during which the worker is working at the employer's disposal carrying out activities or duties, and includes relevant training and travelling time as defined.

Reference periods (reg 4(3), subject to reg 4(4), (5) and to any agreement under reg 23(b)):
  - where a relevant agreement provides for the application of reg 4 to successive periods of 17 weeks, each such period; or
  - in any other case, any period of 17 weeks in the course of the worker's employment.
The default measuring window is therefore 17 weeks. 48 x 17 = 816 hours is the ceiling for a full 17-week reference period — a useful arithmetic cross-check on any rota or hours report.

Computation (reg 4(6)): average working time per seven days = (A + B) / C, where
  A = aggregate hours of working time during the reference period;
  B = aggregate hours of working time in the period beginning immediately after the end of the reference period and ending when the number of days worked in that subsequent period equals the number of excluded days in the reference period;
  C = number of weeks in the reference period.

Excluded days (reg 4(7), current version): days in (a) annual leave taken under reg 13, 13A or 15B; (b) sick leave; (c) maternity, paternity, adoption or parental leave; (d) any period in which the reg 4(1) limit did not apply because the employer had obtained the worker's written agreement. The B element adds hours back for those days, so that absence does not dilute the average and mask long hours.

Employer's duty (reg 4(2)): the employer must take all reasonable steps, in keeping with the need to protect health and safety, to ensure the limit is complied with for each worker to whom it applies, and must keep up-to-date records of all workers who carry out work to which the limit does not apply because the employer has obtained their written agreement.

Worked checks:
  - 17 weeks, 850 hours worked, no excluded days: 850 / 17 = 50.0 hours per seven days -> above 48, breach unless a reg 4(1) agreement (or a Part III exception) applies. Cross-check: 850 > 816.
  - 17 weeks, 700 hours worked plus 10 excluded (sick) days, with 80 hours worked in the following 10 working days: (700 + 80) / 17 = 45.88 -> within the limit.
  - Same 850-hour period with 5 excluded days and 40 hours worked in the following 5 working days: (850 + 40) / 17 = 52.35 -> still above 48; the add-back increases, and does not reduce, the average.

=====================================================================
2. HOW A WORKER IS TAKEN OUTSIDE THE LIMIT — THE STEP
=====================================================================

Identifier: EMPLOYER FIRST OBTAINS THE WORKER'S AGREEMENT IN WRITING (reg 4(1), formerly expressed as "Subject to regulation 5"; reg 5 is headed "Agreement to exclude the maximum").

Single operative step, unpacked from the words of reg 4(1):

  Step: before the worker performs work that would take the average above 48 hours, the employer obtains the worker's agreement, in writing, to perform such work.

Elements, each of which is a condition of the limit not applying:
  1. WHO — the employer must obtain it; the worker must give it. It is an individual agreement between employer and that worker, not a management decision, a works-rule, a rota or a contract term imposed unilaterally.
  2. FORM — "in writing". Oral agreement, or agreement inferred from conduct or from the worker simply continuing to turn up, is not the statutory mechanism. Best practice (and what an inspector or tribunal will look for): a stand-alone, signed and dated document, separate from or clearly identified within the contract, expressly referring to reg 4(1) and the 48-hour average, identifying the work or period covered, and recording that the worker may withdraw.
  3. TIMING — "first obtained". The agreement must pre-date the work. It cannot ratify hours already worked retrospectively; obtaining a signature after the event leaves the earlier period in breach.
  4. SCOPE — "to perform such work". The agreement covers the work it describes; whether it reaches a particular assignment is a question of construction of the document. Open-ended wording is common but should be drafted deliberately.
  5. EFFECT — the limit in reg 4(1) does not apply to that worker for the duration of the agreement. The employer's reg 4(2) "reasonable steps" duty to keep the worker within 48 hours falls away for that worker, and is replaced by the reg 4(2) duty (added by SI 1999/3372) to keep up-to-date records of workers working under such agreements. The agreement does not disapply anything else: night-work limits (reg 6), daily and weekly rest (regs 10-11), rest breaks (reg 12), annual leave (reg 13) and the employer's general health and safety duties continue to apply.
  6. DURATION AND WITHDRAWAL — reg 5 governs the agreement (it may be for an indefinite or a specified period, and may be terminated by the worker on notice; the notice terms are set by reg 5 — see verification note below). Once terminated, the 48-hour average applies again from that point.
  7. PROTECTION — a worker must not be subjected to detriment for refusing to sign, or for withdrawing, such an agreement (reg 31; and see the unfair dismissal protection for that reason). Refusal or withdrawal is not a lawful ground for dismissal or for disadvantaging the worker.

Practical procedure an employer must follow to take a worker outside the limit lawfully:
  a. Identify the workers whose working time, including overtime, would exceed an average of 48 hours per seven days over the applicable reference period (calculate on the (A+B)/C formula, not on weekly totals alone).
  b. Issue the written agreement to each such worker before any such work is performed; obtain the worker's signature and date it.
  c. Record the agreement in a register and keep it up to date (reg 4(2)), so that it is possible to show which workers the limit does not apply to and from when.
  d. Continue to monitor hours; the opt-out removes the 48-hour average, not the night-work, rest and leave entitlements, and not the duty to protect health and safety.
  e. Honour withdrawal on the contractual/statutory notice, update the register, and bring the worker back within the average from that point; take no detrimental action.

=====================================================================
3. ROUTES OUTSIDE REG 4(1) OTHER THAN THE INDIVIDUAL AGREEMENT (for completeness — the question asks how a worker may be taken outside the limit)
=====================================================================
  - A relevant agreement (collective or workforce agreement, reg 23(b)) may provide for reg 4 to apply to successive 17-week periods, and reg 4(5) permits the reference period to be modified by such an agreement — lengthening the window over which the average is struck. This manages the average; it does not raise the 48-hour figure.
  - Part III exceptions remove the reg 4(1) limit entirely in defined cases (excluded sectors, reg 18; domestic service, reg 19; unmeasured working time, reg 20; other special cases, reg 21; shift workers and compensatory rest, reg 22; and the sector-specific provisions). These operate by law and do not depend on the worker's consent.
  - Where the worker has been employed for less than 17 weeks, the reference period is the period elapsed since starting work (reg 4(4)), which changes the measurement window, not the limit.

=====================================================================
4. FLAGS / LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER
=====================================================================
  - Young workers: a separate regime applies (reg 5A, per the instrument's table of contents), and the individual reg 4(1) agreement route is not the mechanism for workers under 18. Do not apply the 48-hour analysis to a young worker without checking regs 5A and 27A.
  - Night workers: the separate 8-hours-per-24 average in reg 6 applies regardless of any reg 4(1) agreement.
  - Enforcement: breach of the 48-hour average without an agreement or exception exposes the employer to improvement/prohibition notices and offences under regs 28-29 and Schedule 3, and to worker remedies under reg 30.
  - VERIFICATION NOTE (honest limitation of the evidence used): the passages relied on reproduce reg 4 in full, its textual amendments (SI 1999/3372; SI 2002/3128; SI 2023/1426) and the instrument's table of contents. They do not reproduce the text of reg 5 (duration/notice terms for the agreement), reg 4(4)-(5) (short-service and extended reference periods), reg 2 (definitions), reg 5A (young workers) or reg 31. Those points are stated above at the level the contents list and the scheme of the instrument support, and should be checked against the current text of those provisions before being relied on in a live matter. Nothing in the two answers given — 48 hours per seven days, averaged; and the employer first obtaining the worker's written agreement — depends on those unchecked provisions.

verdict.summary:
# Record Retention under 21 CFR § 211.180(a) — Batch-Associated Records and the OTC-Without-Expiration-Dating Alternative

## 1. Direct answers

| # | Question | Answer | Clock starts on |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Retention for a production, control, or distribution record required by Part 211 and specifically associated with a batch of a drug product | **At least 1 year after the expiration date of the batch** | The batch's assigned expiration date |
| 2 | Retention for that same record category when the product is a certain OTC drug product lacking expiration dating because it meets the § 211.137 exemption criteria | **3 years after distribution of the batch** | The date the batch is distributed |

Both periods are floors, not ceilings: the regulation says "at least" for the first and imposes a flat 3-year term for the second, and neither displaces any longer period required by another provision, a court order, a consent decree, or a firm's own SOP.

## 2. Governing text (verbatim)

> **§ 211.180 General requirements.**
>
> (a) Any production, control, or distribution record that is required to be maintained in compliance with this part and is specifically associated with a batch of a drug product shall be retained for at least 1 year after the expiration date of the batch or, in the case of certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under § 211.137, 3 years after distribution of the batch.
>
> [43 FR 45077, Sept. 29, 1978, as amended at 60 FR 4091, Jan. 20, 1995]

Source verified against three independent renderings that agree word-for-word:

| Source | Version date | Fetched |
|---|---|---|
| eCFR, 21 CFR 211.180 (current) | current as of fetch | 2026-11-15 |
| GovInfo, CFR-2025-title21-vol4, § 211.180 | 2025-04-01 | 2026-11-15 |
| GovInfo, CFR-2024-title21-vol4, § 211.180 | 2024-04-01 | 2026-11-15 |

Because the current eCFR text and both annual editions are identical and the last amendment is 1995, there is no revision-currency risk in stating the periods as above. No historical revision was requested and none is needed.

## 3. Element-by-element reading of § 211.180(a)

**"Any production, control, or distribution record …"** — covers batch production records, master-production-record-derived executed records, in-process and finished-product control/laboratory records, and distribution records, to the extent Part 211 requires them to be maintained.

**"… that is required to be maintained in compliance with this part …"** — the retention duty attaches only to records Part 211 actually mandates. A record the firm keeps voluntarily is outside the duty (though it becomes discoverable and should be handled under the firm's own retention schedule).

**"… and is specifically associated with a batch of a drug product …"** — the identifying test is batch linkage. Records that are product-level or site-level rather than batch-specific (e.g., the master production and control record under § 211.186, validation reports, annual product reviews) are not governed by this sentence; do not extend the 1-year/3-year figures to them by analogy.

**"… shall be retained for at least 1 year after the expiration date of the batch …"** — the default rule. The anchor is the expiration date printed on the batch's labeling, as assigned from stability data; it is *not* the manufacture date and *not* the distribution date. Because a typical expiration date is already months-to-years after manufacture, the practical retention life of an Rx batch record is (shelf life + 1 year).

**"… or, in the case of certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under § 211.137, 3 years after distribution of the batch."** — the alternative rule. Three conditions must all hold: (i) the product is an OTC drug product; (ii) it lacks expiration dating; and (iii) it lacks expiration dating *because* it meets the § 211.137 exemption criteria. The anchor is distribution of the batch (contrast § 211.180(b), which uses "distribution of the last lot" for components, containers, closures, and labeling — a different provision and a different anchor).

**The two branches are alternatives, not cumulative.** A batch is in one branch or the other. There is no textual basis for reading "3 years after distribution" as a universal floor that also governs expiration-dated products, nor for reading "1 year after expiration" as applying to a product that has no expiration date. Where a firm chooses, as a matter of internal policy, to retain to whichever period ends later, that is a permissible conservative policy because the first branch is expressly a minimum — but it should be labelled policy, not regulation, in the SOP.

## 4. Decision procedure (apply per batch)

1. **Is the record a production, control, or distribution record required to be maintained under Part 211?** If no → § 211.180(a) does not apply; check the governing provision.
2. **Is the record specifically associated with a batch?** If no → out of scope of § 211.180(a).
3. **Does the batch bear an expiration date on its labeling?**
   - **Yes** → retention end date = **expiration date + 1 year**. Go to step 5.
   - **No** → go to step 4.
4. **Is the product an OTC drug product that lacks expiration dating because it meets the § 211.137 exemption criteria?**
   - **Yes** → retention end date = **distribution date of the batch + 3 years**. Go to step 5.
   - **No** (no expiration date but not within the § 211.137 OTC exemption) → see § 7, interpretive gap. Apply a documented, conservative policy and escalate to Regulatory Affairs.
5. **Is any longer period required** by another Part 211 provision (see § 5), a product-specific requirement, a litigation hold, a consent decree, or firm SOP? If yes, the later date governs.
6. **Record the computed destruction-eligible date** on the record-retention schedule at the batch level, and confirm the record remains "readily available for authorized inspection" at the establishment where the activities occurred (or immediately retrievable by computer or other electronic means) for the whole period — § 211.180(c) — and that originals or true copies (photocopy, microfilm, microfiche, or other accurate reproduction) with suitable reader/photocopying equipment are available — § 211.180(d).

## 5. Neighbouring provisions that can extend the period (named, not answered here)

These are flagged so the two figures above are not misapplied; they are outside the requested scope.

- **§ 211.180(b)** — components, drug product containers, closures, and labeling: at least 1 year after the expiration date, or, for § 211.137-exempt OTC products, 3 years after distribution of the **last lot** of drug product incorporating the component or using the container, closure, or labeling. Note the "last lot" anchor; it is not the batch anchor of (a).
- **§ 211.198(b)** — complaint files: until at least 1 year after the expiration date or 1 year after receipt of the complaint, whichever is longer; for § 211.137-exempt OTC products, 3 years after distribution.
- **§ 211.192** investigation records and § 211.180(e) annual product quality review inputs — retention is driven by the record category, but these records frequently sit inside the batch file and therefore inherit the (a) period.
- Any applicable application-based, biologics, or device-drug combination requirement, and any FDA-requested or judicially imposed hold.

## 6. Scoping the OTC branch

The regulation itself defines the carve-out by cross-reference: "certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under § 211.137." The § 211.137 text setting out those exemption criteria was **not** in the retrieved corpus for this task, so this memo does not reproduce or paraphrase the criteria and does not cite § 211.137 paragraph letters. To confirm eligibility for the 3-year branch, read § 211.137 directly in the current eCFR and document the specific exemption basis in the batch record or the retention schedule.

Two practical points that follow from the regulation's own wording:

- **A voluntarily assigned expiration date takes the product out of the second branch.** If a firm prints an expiration date on an otherwise-exempt OTC product, the product no longer "lack[s] expiration dating," and the 1-year-after-expiration rule governs. Firms that assign dates voluntarily should not assume the 3-year term still applies.
- **The exemption must be the reason.** A product that merely has a missing or unassigned expiration date, without meeting the § 211.137 criteria, is not in the second branch. That is a compliance defect in expiration dating, not an eligibility path to the 3-year period.

## 7. Interpretive gap to escalate (not a blocker for either ask)

§ 211.180(a) supplies an express period for (i) batches with expiration dating and (ii) § 211.137-exempt **OTC** products. It does not expressly state a period for a batch that lacks expiration dating for a reason other than the OTC exemption. For such a batch, Regulatory Affairs should adopt and document a conservative position (commonly, apply 3 years after distribution by analogy, or the longest period any arguably applicable provision requires) rather than defaulting to a shorter period. Neither of the two asks turns on this gap.

## 8. Worked examples

| Scenario | Facts | Computation | Retain until at least |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rx solid oral dosage form | Batch expiration date 2027-06-30 | 2027-06-30 + 1 year | **2028-06-30** |
| OTC monograph product within the § 211.137 exemption, no expiration date on labeling | Batch distributed 2026-03-15 | 2026-03-15 + 3 years | **2029-03-15** |
| OTC product that would qualify for the exemption, but firm prints an expiration date of 2028-01-31 | Expiration date assigned | 2028-01-31 + 1 year (first branch governs) | **2029-01-31** |

## 9. Drop-in SOP language

> Batch-associated production, control, and distribution records required by 21 CFR Part 211 shall be retained for at least one (1) year after the expiration date of the batch. For OTC drug products that lack expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under 21 CFR 211.137, such records shall be retained for three (3) years after distribution of the batch. These are minimum periods; where another provision, a regulatory or judicial hold, or this procedure requires a longer period, the longer period applies. Records shall remain readily available for authorized inspection throughout the retention period at the establishment where the recorded activities occurred, or be immediately retrievable by computer or other electronic means, and may be kept as originals or true copies with suitable reader and photocopying equipment available (21 CFR 211.180(c)–(d)).

## 10. Limitations of this answer

- Scoped to § 211.180(a) as requested; § 211.180(b)–(f) and other retention provisions are referenced only to prevent misapplication.
- Based on the current eCFR text and the 2024 and 2025 annual editions, which are identical; no product-specific or jurisdiction-specific assessment is made.
- The § 211.137 exemption criteria are cited by cross-reference only, because that text was not part of the retrieved corpus; confirm eligibility against the current eCFR before relying on the 3-year period for a specific product.

verdict.summary:
# NIST SP 800-63B-4 — Password Length Requirements for Verifiers

## 1. Answers

| # | Question | Value | Normative keyword | Source |
|---|----------|-------|-------------------|--------|
| 1 | Minimum length verifiers must require when the password is the **sole** authentication factor | **15 characters** | SHALL (mandatory) | SP 800-63B-4, §3.1.1.2, Password Verifiers, item 1 |
| 2 | Minimum length when the password is used **only as part of MFA** | **8 characters** | SHALL (mandatory floor); MAY allow shorter than 15 | SP 800-63B-4, §3.1.1.2, item 1 |
| 3 | Maximum length verifiers should **at least permit** | **64 characters** | SHOULD (recommended) | SP 800-63B-4, §3.1.1.2, item 2 |

## 2. Governing text (verbatim)

> "Verifiers and CSPs **SHALL** require passwords that are used as a single-factor authentication mechanism to be a minimum of **15 characters** in length. Verifiers and CSPs **MAY** allow passwords that are only used as part of multi-factor authentication processes to be shorter but **SHALL** require them to be a minimum of **eight characters** in length.
>
> Verifiers and CSPs **SHOULD** permit a maximum password length of **at least 64 characters**."
> — NIST SP 800-63B-4, §3.1.1.2 "Password Verifiers", items 1–2 (final published revision; same text appears in the single-page HTML and the PDF).

Supporting item in the same list (needed to interpret "characters"):

> "Verifiers and CSPs SHOULD accept Unicode [ISO/ISC 10646] characters in passwords. Each **Unicode code point SHALL be counted as a single character** when evaluating password length."

Implementation guidance in the same revision's usability section:

> "Allow at least 64 characters in length to support the use of passphrases. Encourage users to make passwords as lengthy as they want and use any characters that they like (including spaces) to aid memorization. Ensure that user interfaces support sufficient password lengths."

The NIST SP 800-63-4 implementation FAQ restates the change:

> "Minimum password length of 15 characters for passwords being used as a single authentication factor at AAL1 (increased from 8 characters)."

## 3. How to read the three values

**Ask 1 — 15 characters, mandatory.** The SHALL attaches to 15 whenever the password is the single factor. This is the AAL1 password-only case. It is a floor, not a target: verifiers may set their own minimum higher, but must not set it lower.

**Ask 2 — 8 characters, mandatory floor, permitted relaxation.** The MAY relaxes the 15 down to 8 *only* for passwords that are exclusively used inside an MFA process (e.g. AAL2/AAL3 where the password is combined with a cryptographic authenticator). The relaxation is conditional and two-sided: a verifier may keep 15 for MFA passwords, but it may never go below 8. "Only used as part of MFA" is a property of the account/factor configuration, not of the string; a verifier must not apply the 8-character floor to an account that can authenticate with the password alone (no password-only fallback, no "remember this device" path that drops the second factor, no recovery flow that reduces to password-only).

**Ask 3 — 64 characters, SHOULD, "at least".** The recommendation is a *lower bound on the accepted maximum*, not a cap. A verifier that accepts 64 characters satisfies it; a verifier that accepts 100 characters also satisfies it and is closer to the intent ("encourage users to make passwords as lengthy as they want"). A verifier that rejects a 65-character password fails the recommendation. Critically, this is not permission to truncate: accepting a 200-character password and silently hashing only the first 64 characters is a defect (it makes distinct passwords equivalent and is a well-known class of vulnerability).

## 4. Two disambiguations that must not be blended into the answers

**(a) The August 2024 2pd draft says something different and is superseded.** The draft PDF contains: "Verifiers and CSPs SHALL require passwords to be a minimum of eight characters in length and SHOULD require passwords to be a minimum of 15 characters in length." That is the *pre-final* wording (8 = SHALL, 15 = SHOULD). The final published revision inverted this: 15 = SHALL for single-factor, 8 = SHALL floor for MFA-only. Any policy, test, or checklist built from the 2pd draft must be re-based on the final text. Do not cite 2pd for asks 1–2.

**(b) Activation secrets are a different authenticator type.** §3.2.10 covers "a password used locally as an activation factor for a multi-factor authenticator": "Authenticators that use activation secrets SHALL require the secrets to be at least **four** characters in length and SHOULD require the secrets to be at least **six** characters in length." The NIST FAQ calls this out explicitly ("they can be substantially shorter (4 characters rather than 8 or 15)"). This is **not** the answer to ask 2. Ask 2 is about a centrally verified password that is one factor of MFA (§3.1.1.2) → 8. An activation secret (device unlock PIN guarding a stored key, verified locally on the authenticator) → 4/6. A verifier implementing both must keep the two policies in separate code paths with separate constants.

## 5. Verifier-side specification (what to build from these values)

### 5.1 Constants

```
PASSWORD_MIN_LEN_SINGLE_FACTOR = 15   # SHALL  (§3.1.1.2 item 1)
PASSWORD_MIN_LEN_MFA_ONLY      = 8    # SHALL  (§3.1.1.2 item 1) — floor, MAY relax from 15 to this
PASSWORD_MAX_ACCEPTED_MIN      = 64   # SHOULD  (§3.1.1.2 item 2) — accept at least this many
PASSWORD_MAX_ACCEPTED          = 256  # engineering choice, >= 64; not a NIST figure
ACTIVATION_SECRET_MIN_LEN      = 4    # SHALL  (§3.2.10) — separate policy, do not mix
ACTIVATION_SECRET_MIN_LEN_REC  = 6    # SHOULD (§3.2.10)
```

Selecting the minimum at runtime:

```
def required_min_length(account, presented_factor_context):
    # MFA-only relaxation applies only if the password can never be the sole factor
    # for this account, in every flow (login, step-up, recovery, device-trust).
    if account.password_is_sole_factor or account.has_password_only_fallback:
        return PASSWORD_MIN_LEN_SINGLE_FACTOR      # 15
    return PASSWORD_MIN_LEN_MFA_ONLY               # 8
```

Fail-safe rule: if the factor configuration is ambiguous, unknown, or can change at runtime, use 15. Choosing 15 where 8 was allowed is compliant; choosing 8 where 15 was required is a violation.

### 5.2 Length measurement (SHALL: one Unicode code point = one character)

- Measure the **code point count** of the submitted password after the only permitted preprocessing (see 5.4). Do not measure bytes and do not measure UTF-16 code units.
  - Python: `len(pw)` on `str` → code points. ✔
  - JavaScript: `Array.from(pw).length` or `[...pw].length`; `pw.length` counts UTF-16 units and **overcounts** astral characters (an emoji becomes 2). ✘
  - Java: `pw.codePointCount(0, pw.length())`. ✘ for `String.length()`.
  - Go: `utf8.RuneCountInString(pw)`. ✘ for `len(pw)` (bytes).
- Do not NFC/NFKC-normalize before counting or before hashing unless you also hash the normalized form consistently — normalization changes the string and therefore the stored verifier. If you normalize at all, normalize identically on enrollment and verification, and count after normalizing.
- Consequence to accept deliberately: a combining sequence (e.g. `e` + U+0301) counts as 2 characters. This can only help the subscriber reach the minimum; it never lets a shorter password through.

### 5.3 Maximum length handling

- Accept passwords up to at least 64 code points (SHOULD). Accepting 256 is the recommended posture.
- **Never truncate.** If a hard cap exists (e.g. for request-size or hashing-cost reasons), enforce it as a rejection with a clear error at the enrollment/change step, and set it far above 64. Silently truncating to 64 changes the effective password and breaks both security and interoperability with password managers.
- If you use **bcrypt**, note its 72-**byte** input limit. A 64-character password of 3-byte characters is 192 bytes and would be silently truncated by bcrypt. If bcrypt is retained, pre-hash (e.g. HMAC-SHA-256 of the password with a server-side pepper, then bcrypt the digest) or move to Argon2id / scrypt / PBKDF2, which have no such truncation. This is an engineering constraint, not a NIST-stated figure, but it is the single most common way an implementation that "allows 64 characters" actually does not.
- Do not cap length by rejecting long passphrases with composition-style errors; the revision explicitly pushes toward longer, user-chosen secrets.

### 5.4 Interaction with the other §3.1.1.2 rules (must not undermine the lengths)

- The permitted mistyping allowances (trimming leading/trailing whitespace, case-insensitive comparison of the leading character) apply **only if the password remains at least the required minimum length after processing**. Check length *after* trimming, against the same 15 or 8 constant.
- No composition rules (SHALL NOT): never require a digit, symbol, or mixed case. Length is the lever; composition checks would also interact badly with passphrases.
- No periodic rotation (SHALL NOT); force change only on evidence of compromise.
- No stored hints accessible to an unauthenticated claimant (SHALL NOT).
- Accept all printing ASCII plus space (SHOULD) and Unicode (SHOULD); this is what makes 64 characters usable as a passphrase.
- Request passwords only over an authenticated protected channel (SHALL); store salted + hashed with a suitable password hashing scheme, salt ≥ 32 bits, salt and hash both stored, algorithm/cost-factor reference stored, pepper stored separately (SHALL/SHOULD as stated in §3.1.1.2).

1. Open the final published SP 800-63B-4 at `https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/`, section **3.1.1.2 Password Verifiers**.
2. Confirm item 1 reads 15 (single-factor, SHALL) and 8 (MFA-only floor, SHALL, after a MAY to be shorter than 15).
3. Confirm item 2 reads 64 with SHOULD and "at least".
4. Confirm item 4 supplies the code-point counting rule used for both thresholds.
5. Confirm §3.2.10 (activation secrets, 4 SHALL / 6 SHOULD) is a distinct section and is **not** being used for ask 2.
6. Reject any citation to the August 2024 2pd draft (`NIST.SP.800-63B-4.2pd.pdf`) for asks 1–2: that draft's "SHALL 8 / SHOULD 15" wording is superseded by the final text.

## 8. One-line policy statement (drop-in for a security requirements doc)

> Password verifiers SHALL require a minimum of **15 characters** when the password is used as a single authentication factor, and SHALL require a minimum of **8 characters** (and MAY permit fewer than 15) when the password is used only as part of multi-factor authentication. Verifiers SHOULD permit passwords of **at least 64 characters**, counting each Unicode code point as one character, and SHALL NOT truncate longer passwords.

verdict.summary:
VFR FUEL RESERVE FOR AIRPLANES — 14 CFR § 91.151(a)

ANSWER
An airplane may not begin a flight under VFR conditions unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it carries enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and then, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly for at least:

  • DAY:   30 minutes  — § 91.151(a)(1)
  • NIGHT: 45 minutes  — § 91.151(a)(2)

Both figures are flight time at normal cruising speed measured FROM the first point of intended landing, not total endurance and not a fuel quantity. They are minimums; the operator must also satisfy any POH/AFM limitation and any more restrictive operating rule or ops specification that applies.

| Condition when the flight begins | Reserve beyond first point of intended landing | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Day | 30 min at normal cruising speed | 14 CFR § 91.151(a)(1) |
| Night | 45 min at normal cruising speed | 14 CFR § 91.151(a)(2) |
| (Rotorcraft — NOT applicable to airplanes) | 20 min | 14 CFR § 91.151(b) |

REGULATORY TEXT (verbatim, identical in the 2025 XML and 1–1–26 PDF editions of 14 CFR and on eCFR)

"§ 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions.
(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—
(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.
(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

Note that paragraph (b) is the rotorcraft rule; for airplanes it does not apply. There is no VFR alternate-airport fuel requirement — the reserve attaches to the first point of intended landing only.

APPLICATION NOTES
1. Which reserve applies is fixed by when the flight BEGINS, not when it lands. A flight that begins during the day is built to the 30-minute standard even if it lands after dark; a flight that begins at night is built to 45 minutes. Where departure falls on the boundary, use the night (45-minute) figure.
2. "Night" is the § 1.1 definition: the period between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, as published in the Air Almanac and converted to local time. This is NOT the "one hour after sunset" definition used for passenger-carrying currency in § 61.57(b); do not substitute it.
3. "Normal cruising speed" is the cruise speed planned for the flight (normally TAS) at the planned power setting. The regulation fixes the TIME, not the gallons; the fuel quantity follows from the cruise TAS and the cruise fuel flow.
4. "Considering wind and forecast weather conditions" means the reserve must survive the forecast, not still-air conditions — compute the time-to-point-of-intended-landing with forecast winds, then add the reserve time.
5. Do not confuse with § 91.167 (IFR): 45 minutes for airplanes after the alternate. That number coincides with the VFR night figure but is a different rule and does not govern VFR flight.
6. The reserve is a planning minimum, not a target. Landing with exactly the reserve remaining means no margin for a go-around, a runway change, or an unforecast headwind.

FORMAT CONVERSION — reserve expressed as time at normal cruising speed, with distance and fuel equivalents

Reserve time is constant (30/45 min); the distance and fuel it represents scale with cruise TAS and fuel flow.

| Normal cruise TAS | Day 30 min = | Night 45 min = |
|---|---|---|
| 100 kt | 50 NM | 75 NM |
| 120 kt | 60 NM | 90 NM |
| 140 kt | 70 NM | 105 NM |

| Cruise fuel flow | Day 30 min = | Night 45 min = |
|---|---|---|
| 8.5 gph | 4.25 US gal | 6.375 US gal |
| 10 gph | 5.0 US gal | 7.5 US gal |
| 12 gph | 6.0 US gal | 9.0 US gal |

Worked example: 120 KTAS, 10 gph, 180 NM to the first point of intended landing, no wind. Trip fuel 1.5 h = 15.0 gal. Day minimum fuel at start = 15.0 + 5.0 = 20.0 gal (2 h 00 min total endurance). Night minimum fuel at start = 15.0 + 7.5 = 22.5 gal (2 h 15 min total endurance). With a 20 kt headwind the trip becomes 180/100 = 1.8 h = 18.0 gal, so the day minimum becomes 23.0 gal and the night minimum 25.5 gal — the reserve time is unchanged, the trip portion is what moves.

PLANNING CHECKLIST
1. Determine day/night status at the intended start of the flight per § 1.1 civil twilight.
2. Compute time to first point of intended landing using forecast wind and temperature.
3. Add 30 min (day) or 45 min (night) at planned cruise TAS/fuel flow.
4. Compare to usable fuel at brake release; confirm the resulting landing weight and any POH/AFM reserve or tankering limits.
5. Recheck if the departure slips past evening civil twilight — the requirement steps up from 30 to 45 minutes.

verdict.summary:
MEMORANDUM — Timing of individual breach notification under 45 CFR § 164.404(b)

1. SHORT ANSWER

(1) By when: a covered entity must notify each affected individual no later than 60 calendar days after discovery of the breach — and sooner than that if notice can be provided sooner, because the regulation imposes an independent 'without unreasonable delay' obligation.
(2) Standard and outer limit: Standard = 'without unreasonable delay.' Outer limit = 'in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of a breach.' The 60 days is a ceiling, not an entitlement; it does not license using the full period.
(3) Trigger event: 'discovery of a breach,' as defined in § 164.404(a)(2) — the first day the breach is known to the covered entity or, by exercising reasonable diligence, would have been known to it. The clock does not run from the date of the breach itself, and it does not wait for completion of the four-factor risk assessment or of the internal investigation.

2. GOVERNING TEXT

45 CFR § 164.404(b), 'Implementation specification: Timeliness of notification':

  "Except as provided in § 164.412, a covered entity shall provide the notification required by paragraph (a) of this section without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of a breach."

45 CFR § 164.404(a)(1), 'General rule':

  "A covered entity shall, following the discovery of a breach of unsecured protected health information, notify each individual whose unsecured protected health information has been, or is reasonably believed by the covered entity to have been, accessed, acquired, used, or disclosed as a result of such breach."

45 CFR § 164.404(a)(2), 'Breaches treated as discovered':

  "For purposes of paragraph (a)(1) of this section, §§ 164.406(a), and 164.408(a), a breach shall be treated as discovered by a covered entity as of the first day on which such breach is known to the covered entity, or, by exercising reasonable diligence would have been known to the covered entity. A covered entity shall be deemed to have knowledge of a breach if such breach is known, or by exercising reasonable diligence would have been known, to any person, other than the person committing the breach, who is a workforce member or agent of the covered entity (determined in accordance with the federal common law of agency)."

3. ELEMENT-BY-ELEMENT ANALYSIS

3.1 The standard — 'without unreasonable delay'
This is a substantive, separate duty. It requires notification as soon as reasonably practicable under the circumstances. Facts that commonly support a shorter period than 60 days: the breach is contained and scoped early; contact information is already verified; the content of the notice is straightforward. Facts that a regulator may accept as justifying use of more of the window (but never beyond day 60 absent § 164.412): ongoing forensic scoping needed to determine which individuals are affected, or a large affected population requiring mail-house logistics. Investigation alone does not suspend the duty; a covered entity that finishes its investigation on day 20 and mails on day 58 has a 'without unreasonable delay' exposure even though it is inside the outer limit.

3.2 The outer limit — '60 calendar days'
- Unit is calendar days, not business days. Weekends and federal holidays count.
- It is 60 days, not 'two months'; the two diverge (e.g., 60 days from 31 January is 1 April, not 31 March).
- Counting convention: the regulation does not prescribe a counting method. The conservative, defensible method is to treat the day of discovery as day 0 and the sixtieth day thereafter as the last permissible day. Worked examples: discovery Monday 3 March 2025 → day 60 = Friday 2 May 2025 (28 remaining March days + 30 April days + 2 May days = 60). Discovery Monday 15 December 2025 → day 60 = Friday 13 February 2026 (16 + 31 + 13 = 60).
- The deadline is measured by when the covered entity 'provide[s]' the notification, i.e., when it dispatches it, not when the individual receives it. Note on the project's flagged question: the excerpts supplied do not include § 164.404(d)(1) in full and contain no deemed-receipt provision for first-class mail. Do not assume a mailbox rule; build the schedule so that mailing (or other permitted delivery) occurs on or before day 60, with margin for printing and address verification.

3.3 The trigger — 'discovery of a breach'
The clock starts on the first day the breach is known, or by exercising reasonable diligence would have been known, to the covered entity. Three practical consequences:
(a) Constructive discovery. A covered entity that could have known earlier through reasonable diligence is charged with discovery on that earlier date. Delayed log review, unmonitored security alerts, or an unread incident queue can move the start date backwards and put the entity out of compliance on the day it first becomes actually aware.
(b) Imputed knowledge. Knowledge of any workforce member or agent counts — not just the privacy officer or management — unless that person is the one committing the breach. A workforce member's report to a manager, a help-desk ticket, or an agent's notice to the covered entity can start the clock.
(c) The trigger is discovery of the breach, not final determination of every affected individual. Where the population is identified in stages, notice to known affected individuals should not be held back pending identification of the rest; supplemental notice follows for later-identified individuals, each measured from the same discovery date.

3.4 The carve-out in the text — 'Except as provided in § 164.412'
§ 164.404(b) is expressly subject to § 164.412. Background (not verified against the section text, which was not among the supplied excerpts — confirm before relying): § 164.412 permits delay when a law enforcement official determines that notification would impede a criminal investigation, with written determination supporting a specified delay period and oral determinations supporting a brief delay that must be documented. Operational rule: the only lawful basis for going past day 60 is a documented § 164.412 determination. Any delay invoked under § 164.412 should be documented contemporaneously, because the covered entity bears the burden of demonstrating that notifications were made as required, including the necessity of any delay (§ 164.414(b) — also not among the supplied excerpts; confirm).

4. COMPANION DEADLINES (do not confuse with the individual-notice deadline)
- Media notice, § 164.406: for breaches affecting more than 500 residents of a State or jurisdiction, notice to prominent media outlets — same timeliness rule, 'without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of a breach.'
- Secretary notice, § 164.408: for breaches involving 500 or more individuals, notice to HHS contemporaneously with the § 164.404(a) individual notice. For breaches involving fewer than 500 individuals, maintain a log and notify HHS not later than 60 days after the end of the calendar year in which the breaches were discovered.
- Substitute notice, § 164.404(d)(2)(ii): where contact information is insufficient or out of date for 10 or more individuals, substitute notice must be posted conspicuously on the entity's home page for 90 days, or published conspicuously in major print or broadcast media in the relevant geographic areas, and must include a toll-free number active for at least 90 days. Those 90-day figures are durations of the substitute notice itself; they are not extensions of the 60-day deadline — the substitute notice must still be provided within the § 164.404(b) window.
- Urgent situations, § 164.404(d)(3): telephone or other additional notice is permissible, and is in addition to, not in lieu of, the written notice under § 164.404(d)(1).
- Business associate notification to the covered entity under § 164.410 has its own timeliness specification; it is outside the scope of this question and its text was not supplied.

5. OPERATING PROCEDURE FOR SETTING THE DEADLINE
Step 1 — Fix the discovery date. Record the earliest date the breach was known, or by reasonable diligence would have been known, to any workforce member or agent (excluding the person committing the breach). Document the basis. Do not use the date the privacy officer was briefed if an earlier date is supportable.
Step 2 — Start the clock at day 0 on that date. Compute day 60 as the last permissible day, calendar days inclusive of weekends and holidays.
Step 3 — Set the internal target earlier than day 60 to satisfy 'without unreasonable delay' — commonly within a small number of days of completing scoping and confirming addresses, and always with dispatch scheduled to leave margin before day 60.
Step 4 — Confirm the notice content against § 164.404(c)(1) (what happened including breach and discovery dates if known; types of unsecured PHI involved; steps individuals should take; what the entity is doing to investigate, mitigate, and protect against further breaches) and the § 164.404(c)(2) plain-language and formatting requirements.
Step 5 — If any delay beyond day 60 is contemplated, obtain and file a § 164.412 law enforcement determination before the deadline passes; otherwise the deadline is absolute.
Step 6 — Preserve evidence of the discovery date, the dispatch date, and the notice content; the burden of demonstrating timely notification rests with the covered entity.

6. SCOPE NOTE
This memorandum states the federal HIPAA breach-notification timing rule. State breach-notification statutes may impose shorter deadlines or different triggers, and those apply in addition to § 164.404(b). Analysis of any particular incident's discovery date, and the § 164.412 and § 164.414(b) texts, require confirmation against the full regulatory text, which was not included in the excerpts relied on here.
